title: Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper is a position/theoretical piece arguing that contemporary machine learning and AI systems rely on large amounts of human-generated data without adequately crediting or compensating the people who produced it. The author frames this as an unfair “knowledge theft,” claiming that workers and everyday users contribute data that is then used to train profitable AI systems while the original knowledge producers receive no share of the resulting value.

The proposed response is Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence (HIT-AI), a broad paradigm intended to keep humans in the loop by making AI systems more explainable, more traceable, and more accountable for the knowledge they use. The paper emphasizes explainable AI, symbolic and distributed representations, trusted technologies, virtual identity protocols, and privacy-preserving mechanisms as enabling components for identifying which data sources contributed to specific AI decisions.

No empirical study, educational intervention, or learner sample is presented. The paper does not focus on a school-based population; instead, it discusses AI systems in general and speculates about broader labor-market consequences, including mention that chatbots and MOOCs could replace teachers and professors. Its main conclusion is normative: AI should be designed so that knowledge producers can be identified and reimbursed, thereby making AI fairer.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/opinion paper proposing 'Human-in-the-loop AI' as a fairness paradigm. It does not present an empirical study, intervention evaluation, or credible causal methodology, so it fits the lowest evidence tier.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention, learner outcome, or measurable effect is reported. The paper discusses broad AI governance and labor-market implications rather than demonstrated impact in education.
